title: Job 21:17–34
context: Job continues. He asks how often the lamp of the wicked is really put out, and rejects the idea that God simply stores up punishment for their children, insisting that the guilty should feel it themselves. He observes that one dies in full strength and another in bitterness, yet both lie down alike in the dust, and he says that travelers’ reports show the wicked spared and honored even in burial. Job ends by calling the friends’ comfort nonsense; both traditions let his challenge stand as real, while noting lightly that the book and the rest of Scripture speak further of God’s justice.

verses.text: “How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out, that their calamity comes on them, that God distributes sorrows in his anger?
verses.arminianNotes:
Job asks, “How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out,” and whether calamity really comes on them. Arminian readers note that Job challenges Bildad’s claim that “the light of the wicked will be put out” (18:5).

He asks for evidence, not theory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job questioning the friends’ generalization.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that judgment on the wicked is not always visible in this life, and they let Job’s question stand.

verses.text: How often is it that they are as stubble before the wind, as chaff that the storm carries away?
verses.arminianNotes:
Job asks, “How often is it that they are as stubble before the wind,” as chaff carried by the storm. Arminian readers note that Job uses the friends’ own imagery (cf. Ps 1:4) to ask whether it happens as often as they claim.

He does not deny that judgment ever comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job questioning the frequency, not the reality, of judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God will judge, while recognizing that Job’s observation of delayed judgment is honest.

verses.text: You say, ‘God lays up his iniquity for his children.’ Let him recompense it to himself, that he may know it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job cites the friends’ saying, “God lays up his iniquity for his children,” and replies, “Let him recompense it to himself.” Arminian readers note that Job rejects punishment that bypasses the guilty person.

Ezekiel 18:20 also stresses personal responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job objecting to a view that delays justice to the next generation.

Shared ground: both traditions hold that each person is accountable, and both read the verse as Job’s protest against the friends’ explanation.

verses.text: Let his own eyes see his destruction. Let him drink of the wrath of the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Let his own eyes see his destruction. Let him drink of the wrath of the Almighty.” Arminian readers note Job’s demand that the wicked themselves face judgment.

He wants justice that is seen and personal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job longing for visible justice.

Shared ground: both traditions share Job’s longing for justice and see it answered in God’s final judgment, without letting that answer cancel Job’s present complaint.

verses.text: For what does he care for his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off?
verses.arminianNotes:
“For what does he care for his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off?” Arminian readers note that the wicked man is indifferent to what happens after his death.

Punishment on his children would not trouble him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the force of Job’s point.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that Job’s argument exposes a weakness in the friends’ explanation, and they let it stand as part of the book’s honest debate.

verses.text: “Shall any teach God knowledge, since he judges those who are high?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Shall any teach God knowledge, since he judges those who are high?” Arminian readers note that Job affirms God’s wisdom even while questioning the friends.

The line recalls Isaiah 40:13–14.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job acknowledging God as the judge of those who are high.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s reminder that no one, including the friends, can dictate how God must act.

verses.text: One dies in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet.
verses.arminianNotes:
“One dies in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet.” Arminian readers note the picture of a peaceful death.

Job describes it without moral comment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the observation that some die in comfort.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the manner of death does not prove a person’s standing before God, and both let this observation stand.

verses.text: His pails are full of milk. The marrow of his bones is moistened.
verses.arminianNotes:
“His pails are full of milk. The marrow of his bones is moistened.” Arminian readers note the images of health and abundance.

The man dies well-fed and strong.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see prosperity lasting to the end.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s honest description, which challenges any simple link between virtue and comfort.

verses.text: Another dies in bitterness of soul, and never tastes of good.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Another dies in bitterness of soul, and never tastes of good.” Arminian readers note the contrast with the previous verses.

Life’s end varies without clear explanation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the unevenness of human experience.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion for those who suffer to the end, recognizing that Scripture does not hide such lives.

verses.text: They lie down alike in the dust. The worm covers them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They lie down alike in the dust. The worm covers them.” Arminian readers note that death comes to all alike.

Ecclesiastes makes a similar observation (Eccl 8:14; 9:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see death as the common lot of humanity.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that death does not visibly distinguish the righteous from the wicked, and both see in the rest of Scripture a hope beyond the dust, without letting it silence Job’s lament here.

verses.text: “Behold, I know your thoughts, the plans with which you would wrong me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I know your thoughts, the plans with which you would wrong me.” Arminian readers note that Job perceives the friends’ intent to apply their teaching to him.

He sees that their speeches are aimed at him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job naming the friends’ underlying accusation.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Eliphaz will soon make the charge explicit (22:5), which confirms Job’s perception.

verses.text: For you say, ‘Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Job quotes them: “Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?” Arminian readers note that the friends point to the fall of the powerful as proof.

Job suspects the question is directed at his own fallen house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the friends’ argument from visible ruin.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s account of the friends’ reasoning, and they let his objection to it stand.

verses.text: Haven’t you asked wayfaring men? Don’t you know their evidences,
verses.arminianNotes:
Job asks, “Haven’t you asked wayfaring men? Don’t you know their evidences,” and goes on to report what travelers say. Arminian readers note that Job appeals to the wider experience of travelers.

He counters the friends’ appeal to tradition with broader observation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job appealing to evidence beyond the friends’ circle.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that honest observation of the world must be part of wisdom.

verses.text: that the evil man is reserved to the day of calamity, that they are led out to the day of wrath?
verses.arminianNotes:
WEB reads “that the evil man is reserved to the day of calamity, that they are led out to the day of wrath.” Arminian readers note that translations differ on whether this means the wicked are kept for judgment or spared on the day of calamity.

The context suggests Job is describing their escape, though this is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty and do not settle it.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse within Job’s argument that the wicked often escape visible judgment in this life.

verses.text: Who will declare his way to his face? Who will repay him what he has done?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Who will declare his way to his face? Who will repay him what he has done?” Arminian readers note that no one confronts the powerful wicked man.

He seems beyond human accountability.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the apparent absence of justice in this life.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God will repay (cf. Rom 12:19), while recognizing that Job’s question describes real experience in a world where justice is often delayed.

verses.text: Yet he will be borne to the grave. Men will keep watch over the tomb.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet he will be borne to the grave. Men will keep watch over the tomb.” Arminian readers note that the wicked man receives an honored burial.

Even in death he is treated with respect.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the outward honor given to some who lived wickedly.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that human honor is not God’s verdict, and both let Job’s observation stand.

verses.text: The clods of the valley will be sweet to him. All men will draw after him, as there were innumerable before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The clods of the valley will be sweet to him. All men will draw after him.” Arminian readers note the peaceful image of the grave and the crowds who follow.

His end seems gentle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job’s description of a death without visible judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s honest challenge, and both note that Psalm 73:17 speaks of considering the “latter end” of the wicked from God’s sanctuary.

verses.text: So how can you comfort me with nonsense, because in your answers there remains only falsehood?”
verses.arminianNotes:
“So how can you comfort me with nonsense, because in your answers there remains only falsehood?” Arminian readers note Job’s verdict on the friends’ speeches.

The LORD will later say they did not speak rightly of him (42:7).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job rejecting comfort built on a false premise.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that true comfort must be truthful, and both see the friends’ failure as a warning against easy answers to suffering.
